text:
”There's a storyteller,” Rimmon said as they passed near a smaller square. His voice was bright, overly casual. ”I can hear him. Just for a little while?”
Andrej nodded. ”Alright.”
The story was good—a tale of heroes and djinn told by an old man with a booming voice. They settled at the back of the crowd. But Andrej couldn't focus. The words washed over him, meaningless noise. His mind was a trapped bird, beating against the same bars: Nasqu's oily words, the cold press of silver coins, the appointment he was ignoring.
He slipped his hand into his pocket, his fingers tracing the smooth curves of the wooden snake. It was cool and solid, a piece of the past, but even that felt different now. He looked at Rimmon's profile, the rapt attention as he listened to the tale of a hero stealing fire. Rimmon was always the hero in his own head. But where did that leave Andrej? The prize to be won? The treasure to be guarded?
When the story ended and the crowd dispersed, Rimmon turned to him. The forced brightness was gone, replaced by frustrated concern. ”You're not even here,” he said. ”You're just... somewhere else. Worrying.”
”I'm sorry. I'm trying…”
”I know you are.” Rimmon ran a hand through his hair, a gesture of familiar exasperation that now felt charged. ”But, Andrej, you can't let him control you like this. Even when he's not here, he's here.” He tapped his own temple, but his meaning was clear. ”Winning.”
”What am I supposed to do? Just forget?”
”Yes!” Rimmon's voice rose, then dropped to an urgent whisper. ”Or at least try. Because this—” he gestured at Andrej's tense posture, his watchful eyes ”—this is just another kind of cage. You're still hiding. Just in a different way.”
The words struck home. He'd wanted to disappear into the normal crowd, to become a ghost. Rimmon saw it. He always saw too much.
”I don't know how to not be afraid,” Andrej admitted, the confession laid bare between them.
Rimmon's expression softened, but it was edged with a helpless urgency. ”I know. And I'm not saying don't be afraid. I'm just saying... don't let the fear be all you are.” He grabbed Andrej's arm, his grip firm. ”Come on. I have an idea.”
”What kind of idea?”
”The kind that's somewhere between your calm and my chaos.” Rimmon's grin was back, but his eyes were empty. It was a performance, a peace offering. ”Trust me?”
Andrej looked at him, at the boy who smelled of foreign perfumes and spoke of ghosts in his blood. The fracture was there, a hairline crack in everything. But on the other side of it was still Rimmon.
He sighed. ”When you say it like that, I probably shouldn't.”
”But you will anyway.”
”But I will anyway.”
Rimmon led them through a maze of streets with his uncanny sense of direction. They emerged into a medium-sized square, busy but not overwhelming. At the far end, under a faded purple awning, was a small tent. A painted sign showed a hand with an eye in its palm.
”A fortune-teller,” Rimmon announced. ”Perfect, right? Not too exciting for you, not too boring for me.”
Andrej stared. ”You want to know the future?”
”Don't you? Even a little?” Rimmon's eyes were too bright, his energy brittle. ”Come on. What's the harm? It's probably all nonsense anyway.”
Before Andrej could protest, Rimmon was pulling him toward the tent. A woman emerged as if expecting them—forty, lined, beautiful, draped in purple and crimson.
”Two young men seeking wisdom,” she said, her voice low. ”Or perhaps just seeking distraction from their troubles?”
Rimmon's grin was all sharp edges. ”Can it be both?”
She smiled. ”It can be many things. Come.”
The tent was dim, fragrant with intoxicating incense. Cushions, rugs, a low table with cards and bones and a bowl of water.
”Sit.” They sat.
She studied them, her gaze lingering on the space between them as much as on their faces. ”You first,” she said to Rimmon. ”The one who chases. Give me your hand.”
Rimmon extended his hand eagerly. She traced his palm. ”You have a clever tongue. And a heart that burns hot. You see the world as it could be, not as it is. This makes you both blessed and cursed.”
”Blessed how?”
”You will never be satisfied with less than everything. You will build empires or die trying.” Her finger traced a line. ”But you are impatient. You reach for fruit before it ripens.”
Rimmon laughed, a nervous sound. ”That's fair.”
She scattered coloured stones, studied them, her face grave. ”There is someone.”
”There's always someone.”
”Exactly.” Her tone was dry. ”You chase pretty things like a cat chases butterflies—always reaching, never catching. This path leads only to sand in your teeth.”
”Sand in my teeth?” Rimmon's brow furrowed. Andrej watched his friend's bravado begin to crack.
”It means you grasp at beauty and find only emptiness. You pursue desire and find only frustration.” She gathered the stones. ”The butterflies will always fly just beyond your reach, boy. Until you learn to stand still and let them come to you.”
Rimmon looked chastened, vulnerable in a way Andrej rarely saw. ”So... what? I should stop trying?”
